catalog_quote: A Lhomi word is either a high register word or a low register word. This means that the phonation of the vowels is either clear or breathy. This is the salient feature of Lhomi tonology. ... I argue that it is the vowel quality (tense/lax) that is contrastive, not the pitch. High register (tense) words are also more stressed than the low register ones (word stress). These observations need to be either confirmed or refuted by a detailed study. ... He notes that “vowel length is contrastive on the first syllable of disyllabic words, but not on the second syllable. It may be that when the first syllable of a disyllabic word is long it attracts stress, or that the lengthening of the syllable results from its being stressed.” (Ibid., 254). new_statements.rule_in_words: Lhomi is described as a two-register (high/tense-clear vs low/lax-breathy) tone language in which word stress is a correlate rather than an independent contrastive position: high-register words are said to be 'more stressed' than low-register words, and in disyllabic words a long first syllable is heavy and attracts stress (Watters 2002:40 adds that when the first syllable is short both syllables are of roughly equal weight and stress). No fixed-position rule is stated by either source; the stress claims are explicitly hedged as awaiting a detailed study.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; Vesalainen notes 'phonological stress' on the negative prefix (p. 130) and on final question clitics (pp. 139-140, 234), which is emphatic/pragmatic prominence, not a lexical rule. Watters 2002:43-44 says pitch/stress on words like 'moon' vs 'monkey' is not predictable from onset phonation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (mono- and disyllabic citation forms, elicited from Chepuwa-village Lhomi in Vesalainen; Watters 2002 used ~1,000 recorded words from several speakers, Sankhuwa Sabha). Watters 2002 (pp. 40, 43) is the first-hand instrumental basis; Vesalainen 2016 explicitly defers to Watters and adds the register-stress observation.
new_statements.identity_note: Vesalainen's grammar describes the Chepuwa-village dialect of Lhomi (Sankhuwasabha district, Nepal), the reference variety for lhom1239; Watters 2002/2003 describes Lhomi of Sankhuwa Sabha near the Nepal-China border without naming a village. No other variety involved. Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 classify Lhomi as group 68.1 with Thudam (thud1238, now merged into Walungge [ola]) as 68.2.
